stories.title: Ghana: Ghana National Fire Service (Gnfs) Goes Digital
stories.summary: Ghana National Fire Service (Gnfs) Goes Digital 7 September 2026 Ghanaian Times (Accra) With the introduction of the Automated Fire Compliance and Safety System (AFCAS) On a January night in 2025, fire tore through Kantamanto Market in Accra, one of the world's largest secondhand clothing markets, destroying more than 7,000 stalls and upending the livelihoods of over 30,000 traders. Fourteen months later, in April this year, flames swept through the Kejetia Market in Kumasi, one of Ghana's oldest and busiest trading centres. Between the two infernos lay a trail of similar disasters -- Adum, Techiman, the Tamale Timber Market -- each one a fresh reminder that Ghana's relationship with fire safety has, for too long, been reactive rather than preventive. For decades, the country's fire safety regime has rested on paper certificates, manual inspections and a patchwork of enforcement that even the Ghana National Fire Service (GNFS) itself concedes has struggled to keep pace with the scale of the problem. GNFS training materials indicate that more than seven in 10 properties nationwide currently lack a valid fire certificate, that manual processing has typically months, and that paper-based certificates have long been vulnerable to forgery -- leaving no central, real-time record of which buildings, or which extinguishers, actually meet the standard.

She said King Oyowho ascended to the Tooro throne at the age of three and grew into a respected young monarch who carried the hopes and aspirations of his subjects with dignity and commitment. stories.title: 'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'
stories.summary: Image caption, David Etor's first break came after designing and building a kind of "solar oven" in Nigeria By James Diamond ,Â Bristol Â and Â John Darvall ,Â BBC Radio Bristol Published 5 hours ago A Nigerian man has shared the story of how he rose up out of "abject poverty" as a child, to become one of the leading UK academics in his field. David Etor, 43, who grew up in Nigeria, only learned to read and write aged 12 and was told as a child that "nothing good will come out of you", but is now a lecturer in electrical and mechanical engineering at the University of Bristol. He told the BBC how his family was so poor growing up that his mum would pretend to cook food in a kitchen they shared with others, "to protect our integrity" in front of neighbours. "I didn't see a way out," he said. 'The poor called us poor' Speaking to John Darvall on BBC Radio Bristol about the publication of his first book, Etor described growing up in a "compound" with several other families, all sharing a single kitchen, toilet and bathroom. "It was a very poor neighbourhood. We were particularly very poor that the poor neighbours would refer to us as poor," he said. "I do remember that there was a time where my mum would boil water. "[She would] go back in and out, lift the lid, stir the water, go back into the room [and] come back as though she was preparing food... "She would come back in with that pot of water after a couple of hours and it will be as though she's just finished cooking a meal, but it was just water. "She was trying to protect our integrity." More from Bristol Warning issued after dead eels found in brook Published 18 hours ago Childhood pals create 'love letter' to Doctor Who Published 1 day ago Social media inspiring new generation of bookworms Published 1 day ago Etor's first break came whilst doing a kind of national service in Nigeria, when he realised lots of locals were being hospitalised with food poisoning, because they were trying to preserve things by drying them in fields. To solve the problem, he designed and built a kind of "solar oven". "It worked incredibly well," he said, which led to an award from the state government and a job.

stories.title: Angola: Cotton Revival In Busia - Hope Grows Amid Small Farms, Dry Spells And a Silent Ginnery
stories.summary: Angola: Cotton Revival In Busia - Hope Grows Amid Small Farms, Dry Spells And a Silent Ginnery AllAfrica Bonventer Baraza, Manager at Luanda Farmers Cooperative Union Ginnery explains one of the process of cotton linting 6 September 2026 allAfrica.com By Paul Thiong'o The roads leading into the interior of Busia County tell a story of a region that is slowly changing, but perhaps not fast enough. From Luanda to Bumala and Finyula, the journey is punctuated by dusty roads, boda bodas and stretches where getting to the farms is an exercise in patience. Away from the main roads, infrastructure remains a challenge, with motorcycles often providing the only practical means of reaching some farming areas. It is here, amid small farms and modest homesteads, that cotton is quietly making a comeback. But unlike Lamu County, where cotton farmers are taking advantage of the revival of the industry to expand production, farmers in this part of Busia are still growing the crop on very small pieces of land.

stories.title: Is Russia proving better at protecting friends than fighting enemies in West Africa?
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The embrace of Russia by Niger, and other Sahel states, has been seen as a rejection of the post-colonial Western powers By Simi Jolaoso Africa correspondent Published 5 September 2026 When mutinous soldiers seized a strategic military base in Niger's capital last Saturday, the country's ruling junta turned to a foreign partner it has increasingly relied on since coming to power: Russia. Following a night of intense fighting in Niamey, Russia's Africa Corps helped Nigerien loyalist forces to regain control of Air Base 101 at Diori Hamani International Airport. Africa Corps, unlike its predecessor the Wagner Group, is directly under the control of the defence ministry in Moscow. It provides combat support and military training and is thought to have some 200 to 300 men in Niger. Russia's ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropaev, publicly acknowledged the weekend intervention, saying his country's forces had helped "repress a mutiny". "This is seen as a symbolic victory," according to Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at Control Risks. "[One] that will continue to put them at the centre of not just the counter-insurgency campaign, but even in the protection and prolongation of military rule." The attempted coup offers perhaps the clearest evidence yet that Africa Corps' role in three Sahel countries extends beyond its stated mission of helping governments fight jihadist insurgencies.

stories.title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong
stories.summary: Image caption, The Mercator projection is the map widely used across the globe but inaccurately depicts the sizes of countries and continents By Jaroslav Lukiv Published 5 September 2026 Updated 6 September 2026 The UN has just called for the predominant world map to be replaced with one that more accurately reflects the true size of continents such as Africa. The "Correct the Map" resolution adopted by the General Assembly aims to fix the discrepancy with the Mercator map, in which the African continent is shown as being of similar size to Greenland - even though it is in reality about 14 times larger. The UN adopted a new map, the Equal Earth projection, which better represents the true sizes of landmasses - but comes with problems of its own. There have been many prominent attempts over the years to solve the problem of accurately representing the surface of a sphere on a flat rectangle, each with its own benefits and drawbacks. Mercator map Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The Mercator projection has been around since the 16th Century and was vital for navigating the oceans The now widely used Mercator map was created in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator.

stories.title: Sharpeville massacre survivors start legal fight for justice in South Africa
stories.summary: Image caption, Abraham Mofokeng was 20 when he joined a peaceful protest in Sharpeville By Pumza Fihlani Reporting from Sharpeville Published 3 September 2026 Abraham Mofokeng still carries the wounds of the bloody suppression of a protest in South Africa 66 years ago. In what became known as the Sharpeville massacre, police infamously opened fire on thousands of peaceful demonstrators. A bullet is still lodged in Mofokeng's spine, and he has a gentle limp from a gunshot to the leg. "We weren't seen as people," the 86-year-old tells the BBC as he explains the reasons he joined the demonstration on 21 March 1960 against the repressive laws of the white-minority government. "All you were good for was working. You couldn't question them, you were supposed to just do as you're told." The massacre at Sharpeville, which he survived, exposed to the world the violence of the racist apartheid system - yet thanks to an indemnity law passed a year after the killings, none of the perpetrators were ever prosecuted. Mofokeng is now part of a legal case announced on Thursday that will seek to overturn this law.

stories.title: 'The crowd shouted that we'd stolen someone's genitals' - deadly rumours spread on social media
stories.summary: Image source, Alfred Lasteck / BBC Image caption, Boniface Mgala and a friend were pulled out of a restaurant and attacked by a mob that accused them of stealing a man's genitals By Mungai Ngige ,Â BBC Global Disinformation Unit Â and Â Alfred Lasteck ,Â BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Tunduma Published 3 September 2026 More than 80 people were killed between October 2025 and July this year following false accusations about what is termed "genital theft", the BBC Global Disinformation Unit has found after gathering data from police forces across six African countries. The killings are linked to rumours that a simple tap on the shoulder can cause a man's genitals to shrink or disappear. They are being fuelled by widespread misinformation on social media. "They were shouting that we had stolen someone's genitals and we didn't have any way to escape because there was a huge crowd," Tanzanian mechanic Boniface Mgala told the BBC about his ordeal in April when he was badly beaten by those convinced he was a genital thief. His experience was similar to those in videos seen by the BBC: men claim that their genital organs - penis and testicles - have vanished or shrivelled after coming into contact with strangers and a mob then demands that alleged perpetrators return what they have supposedly stolen. Such claims are rooted in longstanding fears and superstitions - and are not new on the continent, particularly in communities where belief in witchcraft remains widespread.

Photograph: Alamy View image in fullscreen A farmer sprays pesticide on sesame fields in Burkina Faso, west Africa. Photograph: Alamy Almost half of world’s farmers poisoned by pesticides every year, experts find Study reveals that pesticide poisoning kills 11,000 people each year, with India accounting for nearly 60% of fatalities Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a study has found. Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network , found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year. Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year.

stories.title: Women behind the lens: ‘The women are moving towards the church, but it is not the final destination’
stories.summary: In her work entitled Holy Gang, artist Puleng Mongale says ‘the sun represents a place where I can meet my ancestors beyond religious limitations’. View image in fullscreen In her work entitled Holy Gang, artist Puleng Mongale says ‘the sun represents a place where I can meet my ancestors beyond religious limitations’. Women behind the lens: ‘The women are moving towards the church, but it is not the final destination’ South African artist Puleng Mongale explores how her childhood church still connects her to the women of her family, not through religion but shared history and memory T his image, called Holy Gang, combines an image of a church in my mother’s home town, Fateng-tse-Ntsho, in Free State province, South Africa , with self-portraits of me, multiplied to form a group of women. Although at first glance the women are moving towards the church, it is not the final destination. Positioned higher, beyond the church, is what appears to be a rising sun.

But I am proud to break the deadly silence around breast cancer in Nigeria Gloria Chinyere Okwu I was told to keep my diagnosis private but I am determined to show the reality of breast cancer and reject the stigma that prevents women seeking treatment ‘M adam, this looks like breast cancer, and if it is, we will chop off your breast.” That was how the doctor welcomed me into the chaotic world of cancer in 2017 when I was 32 years old. He had his back to me, but kept on talking, peering into the specimen bottle.

stories.title: Tunisia's activists decry civil society crackdown
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5JrLK Tunisians have been protesting against President Kais Saied this summer, demanding the restoration of democracy and calling for the release of jailed activists and journalists amid a worsening economic and social crisis Image: Jihed Abidellaoui/REUTERS Advertisement "Most civil society organizations are in a state of shock today," Messaoud Romdhani, a Tunisian human rights activist told DW. "Those who criticize the authorities or situation in Tunisia face widespread repression," he explained, adding that "most have been accused of money laundering, which leads to the suspension of their activities." Another Tunisian activist, who spoke with DW on condition of anonymity, also said that increasingly people were thinking twice before speaking in public or even choosing to work on sensitive issues. "What worries me most is the chilling effect: When organizations face suspension and activists face prosecution or detention , the uncertainty itself becomes a form of pressure," he said. Human Rights Watch has also raised the alarm. In its latest report , published Wednesday morning, the international rights watchdog concludes that Saied is attempting to shutter Tunisia's civil society entirely. "It is clear that the authorities are abusing every tool at their disposal to close the space for civil society in Tunisia," the report reads. The watchdog also points out that civil society groups in Tunisia have played a key role in holding power to account, delivering essential services and advocating for people's human rights . "The government has used abusive, arbitrary prosecutions, detentions, financial investigations and suspension of organizations in an attempt to stifle these voices," Bassam Khawaja, a deputy director in the Middle East and North Africa Division at Human Rights Watch and editor of the report, told DW. He added that it was clear the idea was to shut down all opposition and independent voices in the country. "This amounts to a total crackdown on civil society in Tunisia," he said.

stories.title: Somali piracy surges as the impact of the US-Iran war ripples outwards
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Pirates manage to board ships operating a long way from the coast and then guide them closer to the shore By Barbara Plett Usher Africa correspondent Published 29 August 2026 Updated 31 August 2026 A surge in piracy near Somalia has increased threats to shipping already under pressure from maritime blockades and conflict due to the US war with Iran. Two cargo vessels were seized in the Gulf of Aden within four days last week, rising to at least 13 the number of ships attacked since the start of the year and triggering unprecedented drone strikes against the pirates. It is the biggest escalation in hijackings in more than a decade, renewing concern about security in this region vital to international trade. "Piracy is always a crime of opportunity," says Omar Mahmood, a senior Somalia analyst for the International Crisis Group (ICG), "and right now the pirates see an opportunity." That opportunity comes from the impact of the war on regional waterways further north. Iran and the US continue to battle over control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz. And Tehran's Houthi allies in Yemen have imposed a targeted blockade in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which controls access to the Red Sea.

stories.title: How a South African town cleaned up its polluted river using stones, wood and sand
stories.summary: The Water Hub’s filter beds remove nearly 99% of toxins before most of the water is released back into the river, with some held back to irrigate gardens. Photograph: Courtesy of Water Hub View image in fullscreen The Water Hub’s filter beds remove nearly 99% of toxins before most of the water is released back into the river, with some held back to irrigate gardens. Photograph: Courtesy of Water Hub How a South African town cleaned up its polluted river using stones, wood and sand Scientists say system to treat contaminated wastewater offers a model for ensuring food security in a fast-warming climate A ll it took to turn the murky, heavily polluted waters of South Africa’s Stiebeuel River into a resource clean enough for irrigating a community’s vegetable plots was a collection of stones, heat-treated wood and sand. Without chemicals and using renewable energy, researchers from the University of Cape Town are cleaning 36,000 litres of water, polluted by sewage, chemicals, and traces of drugs and medication, every day to make it usable for growing food in a fast-expanding informal settlement along the course of the river. Scientists behind the project think it could be a model for ensuring food security in the climate crisis. “ What we’re doing is taking that water, treating it every day, and some of that water is now being used for growing vegetables, for feeding hungry children and people living in the informal settlement,” says Kevin Winter, one of the researchers behind the Water Hub project in Langrug , near Stellenbosch in South Africa’s Western Cape region.
